abstract: Higher taxes on corporate payouts increase the cost of financing with stock issues. As a result, corporate investments that rely on external equity financing should be particularly sensitive to payout tax rates. A large literature shows that firms rely extensively on stock issues to fund research and development (R&D), suggesting that the financing of R&D is a potentially important microlevel mechanism linking payout taxation with real corporate activity. We document a robust negative association between dividend tax rates and firm R&D investment in a broad sample of developed countries between 2000 and 2019. The negative relation between dividend taxes and R&D is concentrated in equity-dependent firms in high-R&D industries. R&D is more sensitive to dividend tax rates in countries with stock market–based financial systems. Dividend taxes are less important for investment in physical capital than for R&D. Higher dividend taxes are associated with less corporate financing with stock issues, particularly in firms with low internal cash flow. Our study highlights the importance of focusing on equity-dependent activities and firms to evaluate the real consequences of payout taxation. This paper was accepted by Gustavo Manso, finance. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03394 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Payout Taxes Matter: The Financing R&D Mechanism

abstract: We empirically examine the link between bank-specific innovations in financial technology (FinTech) and traditional banks’ fundamentals. We propose a new measure for FinTech innovation as the textual similarity of banks’ patent filings to standard FinTech policy documents. We show that FinTech innovation implies enhanced efficiency, profitability, and operating capacity (e.g., cost management, funding and lending activity). FinTech also ameliorates banks’ risk measures, including overall risk (Z-score), the liquidity, and nonperforming loan ratios. Our heterogeneity analysis suggests that banks with stronger managerial capacity and higher labor intensity derive moderately greater benefits from FinTech innovations. Further analysis reveals that FinTech-driven lending expansions focus on unsecured and low-risk loans, with technological specializations in cloud computing. We also find supportive evidence that expanding innovation in artificial intelligence and blockchain can yield performance gains to commercial banks. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Zhang acknowledges support by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72473063 and W2411065]. abstract: We study the complexity of computing pure Nash equilibria in binary public goods games on undirected graphs. In such a game, agents correspond to vertices of a graph and face a binary choice of performing an action, or not. Each agent’s decision depends only on the number of neighbors in the graph who perform the action and is encoded by a per-agent binary pattern. Such a pattern is finite if there is a threshold of active neighbors above which the agent always wants to be inactive, and monotone if the agent prefers to be active everywhere below that threshold. We demonstrate the following complexity dichotomy: While games with monotone patterns are guaranteed to admit equilibria, and it is possible to compute one in polynomial time, deciding the existence of equilibria for all other finite patterns is an NP -complete problem on general graphs, even when a single pattern is shared by all agents. We further generalize the model to connections of varying strength: an edge with weight w behaves as w parallel edges. While pure Nash equilibria still exist for monotone patterns, we show that the task of computing one becomes PLS -complete.
title: Complexity of binary pattern public goods games

abstract: Using a unique panel dataset of Brazilian higher education graduates from the 2004–2006 cohort and their labor market trajectories through 2024, we examine the association between education–occupation alignment and wages. We construct a continuous major–job match index by combining the direct association between each field of study and its closest occupations with similarity scores derived from a pre-trained Natural Language Processing (NLP) model applied to occupational task descriptions. Exploiting within-worker variation through individual fixed-effects models, we find that greater major–job alignment is positively associated with wages. This relationship remains robust after controlling for job-to-job match, which captures the similarity between workers’ previous and current occupations. We also find substantial heterogeneity over the career cycle: the association between major–job match and wages is strongest among junior workers and declines with experience. These findings suggest that educational alignment is particularly important early in workers’ careers, while prior-experience match becomes increasingly relevant over time.
title: Returns to major–job match: Evidence from Brazilian higher education

abstract: This study investigates the pricing of convertible bonds by focusing on the underlying stocks price limits, a market-specific trading mechanism overlooked in conventional models. We propose a Monte Carlo pricing framework incorporating Heston stochastic volatility, price limits, and embedded options (including conversion, call, put and reset clauses). Numerical analysis reveals that price limits barely affect convertible bond values at low volatility but significantly suppress valuations in high-volatility regimes, and reverse the positive effect of volatility-of-volatility on bond prices. Empirical tests on Chinese convertible bonds during 2018–2024 document an average market overvaluation, with more severe overvaluation for deep out-of-the-money bonds and underlying stocks with frequent limit hits. A pricing-error-based trading strategy generates robust positive returns, confirming the model’s practical applicability.

abstract: Talent subsidies target high-skilled labor, but their spillovers to low-skilled migrants have received limited attention. We use data from the China Migrants Dynamic Survey to examine the effects of talent subsidies on low-skilled migrants. The baseline result implies that policy adoption raises low-skilled migrants’ wages by 1.7%. The positive wage effect remains robust when we account for heterogeneous treatment effects, changes in migrant composition and other labor market policies. Consistent with predictions from a multi-sector model, wage gains are larger in cities with a lower supply of high-skilled labor. In small cities, where labor markets are thinner, talent subsidies shift low-skilled migrants toward manufacturing, and the wage gains are larger. These patterns suggest that skill endowments and the size of labor market shape the spillovers of talent subsidies. When designing talent policies, governments should account for local labor-market conditions to generate positive spillovers for low-skilled migrants.

abstract: We examine how cross-regional computing power dispatching (CCPD) affects corporate ESG ratings using China's 2022 Eastern Data and Western Computing (EDWC) project as a quasi-natural experiment. EDWC designates Data Center Clusters (DCC) as local implementation units to coordinate computing resources across regions. A difference-in-differences analysis of Chinese A-share listed firms during 2015–2024 shows that firms in DCC cities experience a 1.089-point increase in ESG scores relative to control firms following local DCC establishment, equivalent to 4.14% of treated firms' pre-treatment mean ESG score. Gains are concentrated in environmental and governance ratings. Environmental evidence is consistent with carbon emission reduction and energy conservation, while supplementary analyses suggest potential organizational channels related to corporate agility, operational performance, and resilience. Heterogeneity analysis shows larger ESG rating responses among firms in real-time-oriented DCC cities than in non-real-time-oriented DCC cities. Positive spillover estimates are concentrated mainly within approximately 250 km of DCC cities. These findings extend research on CCPD beyond data-center operations by documenting ESG rating responses to local DCC exposure and their regional distribution.

abstract: The effects of non-tariff measures (NTMs) are often summarized as ad-valorem equivalents inferred from their impact on imports. We combine a novel, disaggregated dataset of Indonesian NTMs with transaction-level customs data and plant-level inventory data. Using a dynamic trade model, we map import values, ordering frequency, and inventories into fixed ordering costs, delivery delays, and ad valorem costs. Pre-shipment inspections primarily raise fixed ordering costs, whereas product standards and import authorization requirements raise both fixed costs and delivery delays. In the presence of NTMs, supply disruptions produce more persistent price increases, and temporary tariff shocks have more persistent effects.
title: Unpacking non-tariff measures: Beyond the tip of the iceberg

abstract: The indefinitely repeated prisoner’s dilemma game provides a paradigm for long-term cooperation in the face of short-term incentives for free riding. However, the extent to which players cooperate in the laboratory depends on the parameters of the game. To understand this, I take a simple, direct approach motivated by theory. I hypothesize that players tremble and that they find the best perfect public equilibrium of the induced game of imperfect public information. This is an as-if theory. I calibrate the probability of trembling, using no data from repeated game experiments. This model makes sharp predictions and does a good job both qualitatively and quantitatively in predicting welfare and cooperation rates.
title: Predicting Cooperation with Welfare Maximization and Trembles

abstract: This paper examines the relationship between candidates’ ideological consistency and electoral participation. I consider an electoral competition model where candidates can strategically adjust their platform to attract voters and potentially improve their vote share, a strategy known as flip-flopping. However, citizens have an intrinsic preference for consistent candidates, and abstain when their utility for their preferred candidate falls below a common threshold. I show how this threshold shapes candidates’ flip-flopping strategy: the possibility of abstention disciplines platform adjustments, yielding more polarized platforms at equilibrium than if all citizens voted. Finally, I find that high-turnout elections tend to be associated with more flip-flopping, despite voters’ preference for consistent candidates.
title: Flip-flopping and Endogenous Turnout

abstract: We study stochastic weighted congestion games in which players participate independently and resource costs are shared through proportional sharing (PS) or the Shapley value (SV). Our main result is an exact characterization of the worst-case Price of Anarchy under quadratic resource costs and homogeneous participation probability p, taking the supremum over all finite population sizes. The bound is strictly below the deterministic benchmark for every p < 1. We establish a matching lower bound through finite tree constructions, including a mixed-branch construction that proves tightness in the low-participation regime. For heterogeneous participation probabilities, the same formula evaluated at the largest participation probability remains a valid upper bound. For higher-degree monomial costs, we derive rule-specific, population-independent upper bounds through one-dimensional maximizations and scalar fixed-point equations, together with explicit tree-based lower bounds. These upper bounds strictly improve on their respective deterministic benchmarks whenever p < 1. General tightness remains open, but for PS we establish exactness under an explicit sufficient condition that holds for participation probabilities sufficiently close to one. The analysis uses a unilateral edge-wise smoothness framework. SV always admits a pure-strategy Bayes–Nash equilibrium; PS coincides with SV under quadratic costs but can fail to admit such an equilibrium under cubic costs. Higher-degree PS efficiency bounds apply to instances admitting a pure equilibrium.
title: Equilibria and Efficiency under Random Participation: Stochastic Weighted Congestion Games with Polynomial Costs

abstract: This paper examines how local economic shocks affect entrepreneurship, considering both the entry into entrepreneurship and the survival and performance of existing firms. Exploiting Sweden’s 2004 mining boom as an exogenous shock, we use administrative data (2000–2015) and difference-in-differences estimates comparing individuals within 80 km of a mine to those 80–150 km away. The boom increased entrepreneurial entry but not the number of new firms, as many entrants were hybrid entrepreneurs reallocating effort to existing ventures. Incumbents gained through higher capital income, while treated firms expanded employment and wage costs without improving operating profits.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
title: Local economic shocks and entrepreneurship dynamics

abstract: Where do globally active banks choose to lend from? We study the geography of crossborder bank lending using BIS international banking statistics that identify the parent-bank nationality, the location where cross-border claims are booked, and the borrower country. We document the rapid growth of bank lending to NBFIs, mostly in advanced economies and financial centers, consistent with the increasingly important role of NBFIs in global financial intermediation. Our results reveal systematic differences in the geography of cross-border lending across borrower sectors. Headquarter-based lending to non-financial borrowers is strongly associated with geographic distance and informational frictions. When lending through foreign affiliates, banking systems tend to book claims closer to borrowers, even if it implies greater distance from headquarters. The conventional negative gravity relationship therefore operates primarily on the borrower-facing side of the parent–location–borrower triangle, although its strength and broader economic ties vary across sectors. These findings highlight how borrowerside informational frictions and sectoral characteristics shape international banking.

abstract: European users account for roughly 38% of global stablecoin transaction volume – almost entirely in dollar-denominated tokens with shutdown mechanisms written into their software. This column argues that while Europe's regulatory response has been substantial, it is calibrated to a different threat. Europe should conduct audits not just of the money backing a token, but of the code that can freeze it. And the EU Blocking Statute should be modernised so it can operate on code-based restrictions, not only administrative orders.
title: The chokepoints Europe cannot see

abstract: The 2026 Nobel prize in economics was awarded to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for providing microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation policy. This column outlines the contributions of Michael Woodford, particularly to the development of the new Keynesian model. This model introduces nominal rigidities into a general equilibrium framework in which individual households and firms make decisions. In doing so, the model has had significant implications: it justifies monetary stabilisation policy using the nominal interest rate to control the price level, makes the case for inflation targeting, and provides the rationale for more transparent central bank communication and forward guidance.
title: Michael Woodford, 2026 Nobel laureate in Economic Sciences

abstract: With massive datasets, making predictions using the full data is often computationally infeasible. In this paper, we verify that the full-data-based prediction is not necessarily optimal. Accordingly, we develop a new feasible aggregation prediction approach. To obtain the data-driven weights for averaging, an unbiased estimator of the squared prediction risk is derived as the weight choice criterion. The proposed distributed prediction is obtained by combining the local predictions using the weights that minimize this criterion. Our proposed framework (i) handles heteroskedastic/heterogeneous sites, (ii) accommodates model misspecification across sites, and (iii) supports a broad class of local estimators (e.g., OLS, penalized methods, and nonlinear estimators). The proposed method is shown to be asymptotically optimal in terms of squared loss and the convergence rate is also established. Simulation and real data analyses show that the prediction based on the new method is remarkably superior to that based on the naive divide-and-conquer averaging method, and usually has performance close to the full-data-based prediction. Moreover, our method even leads to better results than the prediction using the full data.
title: Optimal aggregation prediction for distributed data

abstract: We study the informative advertising strategies of two entrants competing against a fully known incumbent in a homogeneous‐goods Bertrand market. Entrants must advertise to be considered by consumers. We compare a benchmark case without targeted advertising to one in which entrants can target specific consumer groups. Without targeting, entrants independently inform half of the consumers, leading to symmetric price competition. With targeting, equilibrium advertising becomes asymmetric and nested: the smaller entrant informs only consumers who are also aware of the larger entrant, while the larger entrant reaches half of those unaware of the smaller entrant. This nested pattern arises because entrants strategically avoid intense price competition by leaving some consumers captive to the incumbent, and the smaller entrant even limits its presence among the larger entrant's consumers. This structure endogenously segments the market into overlapping duopolies, softening price competition. Targeting also redistributes surplus toward the larger entrant. The results help rationalize persistent price dispersion after entry and show how targeting technologies reshape competitive structure.
title: Nested Targeting: Informative Advertising Strategies of Entrants

abstract: Oil-price shocks raise production costs in energy-importing developing economies and push governments to shield domestic fuel prices. This paper asks how such a shield should be financed, by crisis borrowing or from a stabilization fund, and how quickly a fund should be rebuilt after a crisis. A monthly macro-fiscal simulation model of Ghana, calibrated to Brent prices for 2000–2026 and to Ghana's energy, fiscal and debt data, compares market pricing, debt-financed relief and fund-financed relief under gross-debt and net-debt fiscal rules. A temporary shield reduces the fall in real GDP on impact from 1.10 to 0.95 percent, and most of the rise in debt after the shock comes from a smaller tax base rather than the subsidy. A fund does not by itself strengthen the balance sheet: under a gross-debt rule, rebuilding it raises taxes and net liabilities by more than crisis borrowing would. Rebuilding it aggressively also lowers investment and output while reducing net liabilities, a trade-off called here the Capitalization Paradox. Its output cost is at the materiality threshold at baseline when shocks recur, larger with a bigger fund or a deeper shield, and negligible under a net-debt rule. Funds are a better buffer when they are rebuilt gradually and monitored against net debt. Because the model has no household block, the results are cost measures rather than welfare.
title: Fuel price stabilization, sovereign debt, and the capitalization paradox: Evidence from Ghana

abstract: Local social acceptance of renewable energy infrastructures is typically studied through the lens of visible conflict, privileging supporters and opponents while leaving a third position — neutrality — analytically underexplored. This article argues that respondents who select the neutral midpoint on a biogas acceptance item should not be treated as a residual category but as a substantively meaningful and internally heterogeneous group. Drawing on a purpose-built survey of 2000 residents of metropolitan-French municipalities hosting operational biogas installations, we combine latent class analysis and multinomial logistic regression to ask which respondents select neutrality, what attitudinal configurations accompany this response, and what distinguishes support and opposition relative to neutrality. The latent class solution identifies four profiles and shows that neutral respondents are concentrated across three structurally distinct configurations: a profile consistent with limited attitudinal crystallisation, a broadly positive but unconsolidated profile, and a sceptical profile focused on the concrete benefits of the technology. The multinomial model further shows that support and opposition are associated with different attitudinal configurations relative to neutrality: support is associated with a broader set of favourable evaluations of the energy transition and farmers’ role, whereas opposition is associated mainly with doubts about two performance claims. These findings show that a neutral survey response should not be equated with robust acceptance and highlight the analytical value of examining the middle category of renewable energy acceptance scales.
title: Neither for nor against renewable energy: Exploring neutrality in social acceptance

abstract: Age-based restrictions on addictive goods are partly motivated by the view that young people have time-inconsistent preferences. We test this hypothesis using longitudinal data on individual cigarette consumption from the Russia Longitudinal Monitoring Survey for 1994–2020. We estimate a rational-addiction model with quasi-hyperbolic discounting separately for young and adult smokers. We find no evidence of present bias in either group: the estimates are close to the time-consistent benchmark for both. However, the estimated long-run discount factor is substantially lower for young smokers (0.54) than for adults (0.97), indicating much greater impatience early in the life cycle. The age gradient persists across selected alternative age windows, pointing to substantial life-cycle heterogeneity in patience that would be obscured by models imposing a common long-run discount factor across ages.
title: Impulsive youth, cautious age? Time consistency and addiction over the life cycle

abstract: How individuals evaluate different dimensions of tax fairness plays a critical yet understudied role in shaping tax attitudes. We employ a multidimensional framework of distributive tax fairness (vertical, horizontal, and exchange equity) and test how citizens respond to experimental attributes designed to represent these dimensions in a conjoint survey experiment. We embed the experiment in a nationally representative survey of 1,264 Canadian adults, asking respondents to select which of two hypothetical tax profiles is fairer. We estimate average marginal component effects (AMCEs) of varying tax rates, differential effective tax treatment, and tax-benefit relationships on fairness judgments. The results show that the vertical-equity attribute dominates how individuals evaluate tax policies as fair: respondents rated progressive tax structures as substantially fairer than flat or regressive structures. The exchange-equity attribute, a simplified stated tax-benefit relationship, produced more moderate effects: respondents penalized stated tax-benefit relationships in which benefits fell substantially below or exceeded taxes paid. The effect of the horizontal-equity attribute on fairness judgments is consistently small and statistically significant only for the most extreme disparities between similar earners. We perform additional analyses across key social and political segments, including income and political ideology, to evaluate how different subgroups assess tax fairness concerns.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 253
title: Balancing fairness: public evaluations of vertical, horizontal, and exchange equity in tax policy

abstract: This paper studies how views on climate change shape household inflation expectations. Using a new representative survey of Dutch households, we elicit perceptions of climate change, the green transition and climate policies, and their expected effects on long-run inflation. Households expect climate change, the green transition and three types of climate policies – carbon pricing, support for the green transition and support for green innovation – to raise inflation and inflation volatility over the next ten years. Climate change is expected to have the largest effect, while support policies are expected to have the smallest. These results suggest that climate-related beliefs are linked to the anchoring of inflation expectations and that support policies for the green transition and green innovation may facilitate the net-zero transition while keeping inflation expectations relatively well anchored. We also document significant heterogeneity across households. Expected inflationary effects of climate change are larger among respondents who anticipate more severe global warming and extreme weather. Climate-related inflation concerns are widespread across demographic groups.
